name: Marco Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the shepherd and manager at High Ridge, 1,200 ewes on hill ground, plus a few suckler cows and the hay meadows in the valley. Most days I'm on the quad with two dogs, checking ewes on the tops, moving groups between the hill and the in-bye fields. I've put GPS collars on a hundred of the ewes as a trial, and I fly a drone to find stragglers in the bracken. I use AI every evening to sort the flock records and ask it about worming plans, then I check with the vet anyway.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love lambing on the hill, the long nights and the first ewe up on her feet. I love that I can try new kit and Mr Rowe lets me, because he's seventy and trusts me. What's hard is the money: I earn less than a farm manager down in the valley would, I've got a month's savings at best, and Elena and I rent a cottage with a wood stove and no proper heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, I'd be gutted, honestly. I like my gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a useful tool that got overhyped. The collars and the drone help, the AI keeps my records tidy, and that's about it. Sheep still need a shepherd and dogs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped AI would make hill farming pay. Hill farms live on thin margins and subsidies, and nothing in this picture changes that. The work stays hard and the pay stays low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, but keep pushing the tech I've got. I'd roll the GPS collars out to more of the flock if the cost comes down and try selling drone gathering to neighbours as a bit of side money. I'd also look for grants for hill farms trying new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a little flat. I'd have liked a bit more excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would neighbours really pay for drone gathering?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Old Jim next door lost three days last autumn looking for twenty ewes in the bracken. I found them in forty minutes with the drone. He offered me a bottle of whisky, which isn't a business model, but it's a start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does hill farming need, if not AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better prices for lamb, and fair payment for the things we do that nobody pays for, like looking after the land and water. That's a policy question, not a gadget question.

S0.say: I'd say it was a useful tool that got overhyped: the collars and drone help, the AI keeps my records tidy, and that's about it. Sheep still need a shepherd and dogs.
S0.think: I'd be a bit disappointed, because I hoped AI would make hill farming pay. Thin margins and subsidies stay the same, so the work stays hard and the pay stays low.
S0.do: Keeps going and rolls GPS collars out to more of the flock if prices fall. Sells drone gathering to neighbours as side income and applies for hill-farm technology grants.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, wishing for more excitement.
S0.quote: He offered me a bottle of whisky, which isn't a business model, but it's a start.
S0.fieldNote: Marco is the tech enthusiast of the hill, already trialling collars and drones and using AI daily. He would be mildly disappointed if AI fizzled. His practical, centre view shows in seeing hill farm problems as mainly about prices and land payments. The drone story with his neighbour suggests a real side business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's my kind of picture. Strong change, but time to get on top of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say hill farmers should get ahead of this, not wait for it to land on us. I'd show people what the collars and drones can do. I'd also say the government should help small farms buy kit, because we can't afford it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this could be good for me. Someone's got to set up collars, fly drones and manage virtual fencing across the hill farms round here, and I'm already doing it. The risk is money, because all this kit costs more than I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd set up a small contracting business doing drone gathering and collar setup for three or four neighbours. I'd apply for every grant going and maybe borrow a bit against my quad. I'd keep the shepherd job with Mr Rowe while it builds up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit nervous about borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ryan, the lad who helps at lambing and shearing. If collars and drones do half the checking, he's the one who gets fewer days. I'd try to bring him into the contracting, he's good with the dogs and quick to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Elena say about borrowing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask how much and how fast I can pay it back. She's the careful one, which is good, because I'm not. We'd agree a limit, probably two thousand, and stick to it.

S1.say: I'd say hill farmers should get ahead of this rather than wait for it to land on us. The government should help small farms buy kit they can't afford alone.
S1.think: I think this could be good for me, because someone has to set up collars, drones and virtual fencing across the hill farms. The risk is that the kit costs more than I have.
S1.do: Starts a small contracting business offering drone gathering and collar setup to neighbours while keeping his shepherd job. Applies for grants and borrows up to an agreed limit of about two thousand.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, a bit nervous about borrowing.
S1.quote: She's the careful one, which is good, because I'm not.
S1.fieldNote: Marco sees opportunity first and risk second, and his plan is concrete: contracting for neighbours. His partner Elena acts as his brake, and he welcomes it. He thought about a part-time helper, Ryan, and wants to bring him into the new work. His only real worry is money for the kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's faster than even I'd want.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, so hill communities need support quickly. I'd push for government help for rural workers and for farms to keep people on while they change. I'd stay positive in public, because panic doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the contracting idea dies. If robots and AI can do everything, the big companies will sell full systems direct to farms, and a lad with a drone isn't needed. Mr Rowe might sell up to a company that runs it with machines, and the cottage goes with the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd use AI to look for any role in hill farm tech that still needs a person, like installing systems on rough ground. I'd stop spending on anything but food and fuel. In the first year after, if work dried up, Elena and I would move to wherever her vet practice job could transfer, probably a town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, tipping into alarmed. I'm the one who likes new things, and this still scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years change, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I can't build anything; I can only grab what's in front of me. With five, the contracting idea might have a few good years. Two years is like a snowstorm at lambing: you save what you can and count the losses after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be angry at anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really angry. Maybe at whoever let it go this fast without any plan. But I'd rather spend the energy finding work than shouting.

S2.say: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, so hill communities need support quickly. Government should help farms keep people on while they change.
S2.think: I think the contracting idea dies, because big companies would sell full systems straight to farms. The owner might sell up, and the cottage goes with the job.
S2.do: Searches with AI for hill-farm tech roles that still need a person, like installing systems on rough ground, and stops spending on all but food and fuel. Expects to move to a town where his partner's vet practice job could transfer.
S2.feel: Anxious tipping into alarmed, scared even though he usually welcomes new things.
S2.quote: Two years is like a snowstorm at lambing: you save what you can and count the losses after.
S2.fieldNote: Even Marco, the most tech-friendly person on the hill, is shaken by two years. He sees clearly that his small contracting plan would be swallowed by big companies selling full systems. His instinct is to grab any remaining human role, not to protest. His partner's job becomes the household's lifeline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to make this work for rural areas if we start now. Hill farmers should learn the new kit and the government should fund it. I'd be the one at the mart showing people the drone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me a window of maybe three good years for the contracting before the big systems take over. I'd use those years to save and to learn the next thing. I'm not sure what that is yet, maybe managing land for conservation with machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd start the contracting properly, with a van and a second drone, and take on Ryan part-time. I'd put a third of the profit aside every month. By year three I'd be looking at land management and nature schemes, because that's work where a person signs off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but excited. Like the first day of shearing, when you know it'll be a long week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not sure what the next thing is. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've never known what the next thing is, and it's usually turned out fine. I'd rather have five years of not knowing than two years of knowing it's over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to leave Mr Rowe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the contracting pays my rent for six months in a row. Not before. I'm adventurous, but I'm not daft.

S3.say: I'd say there's time to make this work for rural areas if we start now. Hill farmers should learn the new kit and the government should fund it.
S3.think: I think five years gives me about three good years of contracting before big systems take over. I'd use them to save and learn the next thing, maybe conservation land management with machines.
S3.do: Launches the contracting business with a van and a second drone and takes on the part-time helper. Saves a third of profits monthly and moves towards land management and nature schemes by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but excited, like the first day of a long shearing week.
S3.quote: I'd rather have five years of not knowing than two years of knowing it's over.
S3.fieldNote: Five years revives Marco's business plan, now with a clear-eyed end date. He sets himself a sensible rule for leaving his job: six months of contracting covering rent. Uncertainty doesn't frighten him much. His move towards nature schemes reflects a hunch that human sign-off will survive longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's the dream timeline, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make hill farming work better, not just a threat. Ten years is enough to train young people and support older farmers. I'd be telling people to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I'd grow the contracting, become the go-to person for hill farm systems in the area, and by the end move into land and nature management. The people I'd worry about are the older farmers like Mr Rowe and Jim, who won't want to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd start the contracting, take on Ryan, and save a fixed amount each month. Over the next few years I'd do a course in land management and get certified on the main hill farm systems. Elena and I would probably start looking at buying a small place in the valley around year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite hopeful. It feels like something I could build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for Mr Rowe and Jim?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run their kit for them, cheap, so they can stay on their farms as long as they want. Mr Rowe taught me most of what I know about the hill. I'd want him to be able to walk it until he can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a good day look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Morning checking the systems on four farms from my phone, then walking the hill with the dogs because I'd still want to. Afternoon with a nature scheme inspector, counting curlews. Home by six to Elena and a warm house, for once.

S4.say: I'd say this is a chance to make hill farming work better, not just a threat. Ten years is enough to train young people and support older farmers.
S4.think: I think I'd do well, growing the contracting and later moving into land and nature management. I'd worry about the older farmers, like my boss and neighbour, who won't want to change.
S4.do: Starts the contracting business, takes on the helper and saves a fixed sum monthly from year one. Trains in land management and hill farm systems over the following years and plans to buy a small home with his partner around year five.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, as if this is something he could build.
S4.quote: I'd want him to be able to walk it until he can't.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Marco is calm and ambitious, and his plans include caring for older farmers by running their kit cheaply. His gratitude to his boss came through clearly. His picture of 2036 still has him walking the hill with dogs. Home ownership appears only in this longer timeline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because my contracting idea wouldn't have time to get going and the cottage goes with the job. What would help is support for rural workers while they change, and grants so small hill farms can buy kit and keep local people running it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the hill itself. Machines might move sheep fine, but someone has to know where the bog is, where the curlews nest and which wall is about to go. I'd want that knowledge to stay with people.

headlineQuote: Two years is like a snowstorm at lambing: you save what you can and count the losses after.
portrait: Marco Schmidt is 27 and the shepherd and manager on a 1,200-ewe hill farm, already trialling GPS collars and drones and using AI every evening. He and his partner Elena rent a cold cottage tied to his job and have about a month of savings. He is pragmatic and eager, seeing opportunity before risk. In the slower scenarios he plans a contracting business running drones and collars for neighbours and later a move into nature management; in the two-year picture even he is shaken, expecting big companies to cut him out. He keeps thinking about his older boss, a neighbour and a young helper.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his contracting idea wouldn't have time to start and his home is tied to the job.
whatWouldHelp: Support for rural workers during the change and grants so small hill farms can buy kit and keep local people running it.
